text: Think about the last time a colleague looked at your work and told you,
good idea.
Why did you get that reaction?
You likely received that compliment because you saw something they missed,
connected things in a new way, or found a better way to move forward.
That is creative thinking.
It's the ability to see a problem differently,
question the obvious approach, and find an angle other people missed.
We often make the mistake of reserving the word creative for artists, writers, and musicians,
but that definition is far too narrow.
It applies to anyone who solves problems or imagines a better way.
Consider Steve Jobs.
He didn't build his business empire by painting or composing music.
He helped build Apple by seeing that computers could be simpler, more personal, and easier to use.
He noticed a possibility that the rest of the industry had overlooked.
His success came from applying a different angle to an existing technical problem.
This board lays out exactly who thinks creatively.
You'll notice these are highly structured, rule-bound professions.
A lawyer finds a strategy nobody else saw in the same case file.
They use the same laws and facts, but take a different approach.
An entrepreneur spots a need everyone else overlooked and builds a new way to meet it.
An engineer finds a solution when the standard approach cannot solve the problem.
A doctor looks at the same symptoms and considers a diagnosis others missed.
Creativity is not a job title or a personality trait.
It is a habit of thinking that runs underneath any job where the standard answer is not enough.
Today, AI gives polished answers in seconds.
A professional advantage moves to the person who can notice what is missing,
connect ideas from different places, and choose the better direction.
Creative thinking is a set of habits that you can improve.
This image breaks down four actionable ways to practice those habits.
First, generate before you judge.
List several ideas, including bad ones, before deciding what works.
The obvious ideas usually arrive first.
Second, ask what if.
Change one rule or assumption.
Ask what would happen if the opposite were true.
Third, connect unrelated things.
Borrow a pattern, feature, or approach from somewhere completely different and apply it to the problem.
Finally, step away, then return.
Work on the problem, then take a walk or switch activities.
New connections often appear after your attention moves elsewhere.
These four habits widen your options, then judgment picks the one that fits.
AI widens the options, you still pick the better angle.
